Allele. These are alternative versions of a gene at the same locus on a chromosome, differing in their DNA sequence and often producing different phenotypic outcomes. Most genes exist in multiple alleles within a population, and an individual carries two copies—one from each parent—determining their phenotype through dominance relationships. Alleles are the units of inheritance whose frequencies change under selection, mutation, and genetic drift, driving evolution and genetic diversity.

Each gene on a chromosome exists as one allele per chromosome. Diploid organisms carry two copies, homozygous if identical and heterozygous if different. Alleles arise through mutation. Any change to DNA sequence at a locus generates a new allele—whether through substitution, insertion, deletion, or duplication. Allele frequency, often represented as p or q, is the proportion in a population. Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium predicts genotype frequencies from allele frequencies in the absence of evolutionary forces.

Dominant alleles mask recessive phenotypes in heterozygotes, while recessive alleles express only when homozygous. Importantly, dominance is defined by the phenotype, not the allele itself. In incomplete dominance, heterozygotes show an intermediate phenotype—neither parental type. Codominance presents a different pattern, where both parental traits appear simultaneously in heterozygotes. Population genetics tracks how allele frequencies change through selection, where favored alleles increase and unfavored ones decline. Genetic drift causes random sampling in small populations, and mutation and migration also shape these frequencies.

Mendel inferred alleles from pea-plant breeding ratios, calling them factors. The term allele was formally coined by Hugo de Vries in the nineteen hundreds. A selection coefficient quantifies the fitness cost of an allele, and selection intensity depends on this coefficient and allele frequency, making rare alleles harder to purge. Multiple alleles can coexist in a population—the ABO blood group has three alleles, and HLA loci show around ten thousand known alleles, diversity maintained by selection and mutation-drift balance. Balancing selection maintains multiple alleles, such as heterozygote advantage in sickle-cell trait, and frequency-dependent selection also preserves allelic variation. Loss of alleles reduces population genetic variation, and allele frequency change is the essence of evolution at the molecular level. These are the genetic building blocks that connect to a locus, determining expression through heredity and mutation.
